evidence_set: Reaction time was slower in three naturalistic studies, and three laboratory studies found no evidence of slowing; pooled over five studies, g = 0.66 (0.31 to 1.00), I2 = 36%, P < 0.001. One of those laboratory studies could not be pooled for lack of information, which the authors say may inflate the estimate.

During a simulated commute, divided-attention response time was slower on the morning after a night of social drinking than after a night without alcohol: 3.5 (SD 1.8) against 2.4 (1.3) in all 52 drivers, d = 0.55 (ANOVA F(1,50) = 15.6, p < 0.0001), and 3.4 (1.6) against 2.3 (1.0) in the 26 with zero breath alcohol, d = 0.69.

evidence_set: In all 52 drivers, eight of 15 driving measures were worse on the morning after drinking than on the morning after a night without alcohol: divided-attention response time 3.5 (SD 1.8) against 2.4 (1.3), d = 0.55; incorrect and missed responses d = 0.21 and 0.30; mean speed 35.9 against 31.7 mph, d = 0.42; centre-line crossings 7.8% against 4.0%, d = 0.36; time off road 1.6% against 0.6%, d = 0.68; lane excursions 18.9 against 10.6, d = 0.58; tickets 1.2 against 0.8, d = 0.34.

In the 26 drivers with zero breath alcohol, morning after drinking against morning after a night without alcohol: response time 3.4 against 2.3, d = 0.69; mean speed 33.7 against 29.1 mph, d = 0.40; centre-line crossings 6.0% against 3.8%, d = 0.48; time off road 1.3% against 0.5%, d = 0.61; lane excursions 20.2 against 9.7, d = 0.64; collisions 1.1 against 1.6, not significant.

Lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), speed variability, mean lane position and speed-limit exceedances did not differ significantly between the two mornings in all 52 drivers; for collisions (1.8 against 1.3) the ANOVA alcohol effect was significant (p = 0.04) but the paired comparison was not. Lane deviation appears to be the SDLP listed in the Methods, the principal measure of the 'gold standard' highway test.

Drivers with residual breath alcohol had more collisions on the morning after drinking than on their alcohol-free morning (2.5 against 0.9, d = 0.74), the only driving measure with an alcohol-by-group interaction. The authors attribute the residual group's faster driving, more speed-limit exceedances and more tickets to residual alcohol, but that group also drove faster, exceeded limits more and got more tickets on the alcohol-free morning (34.3 against 29.1 mph; 10.4 against 7.0 exceedances; 1.0 against 0.6 tickets), so these group differences cannot be attributed to residual alcohol (editors' note).

Drinking was unobserved and amounts are not reported (some participants could not recall them); sleep was not recorded, and the authors note that sleep loss may be a significant component of hangover effects on next-day performance. Their statement that the impairment is equivalent to driving at or above 0.05-0.08% blood alcohol cites another study's simulated highway test (ref 21); no alcohol benchmark was run in this study.

evidence_set: Primary outcome: total Hangover Symptoms Scale score did not differ significantly between NAC and placebo (median 10 against 13, P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache (1 against 1, P = 0.93), nausea (0 against 1, P = 0.11) and weakness (1 against 1, P = 0.72) did not differ significantly either.

A subset of five valid items gave the same result: median 5 (range 0 to 19) with NAC against 5.5 (0 to 20) with placebo, P = 0.86 (analysed as independent groups with Mann-Whitney tests; 91 observations against 98 expected from 49 completers in two sessions, editors' calculation).

evidence_set: Self-reported minutes to fall asleep (36.5 with caffeine against 23.2 without), minutes asleep (390.7 against 404.7) and Stanford Sleepiness (2.52 against 2.78) did not differ significantly (d = 0.28, 0.21, 0.23).

The caffeine group rated average sleep quality better than the group given beer without caffeine (4.45, SD 0.41, against 4.16, SD 0.49; t(62) = 2.49; d = 0.64); split afterwards, the difference lay more in morning alertness and concentration items (d = 0.42, p < 0.10) than in night-time items (d = 0.30).

evidence_set: Five trials (551 on acetaminophen, 350 on placebo) were pooled with a fixed-effect model: the difference in mean change in ALT is printed as 0.0 IU/L (-0.2 to 0.1; labelled '97% CI' in the Results and '95%CI' in the Abstract), Q = 1.7, I2 = 0. Recalculated from Table 1, these figures are a standardized difference (-0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.10), as the forest-plot legend says; in IU/L the pooled difference is 0.09 (95% CI -1.27 to 1.46) (editors' calculation).

At later, unpooled measurements ALT was higher with acetaminophen than placebo by 12.6 IU/L (Dart 2010) and 8.4 IU/L (Heard 2007, statistically significant), mostly just after the end of dosing, and by 18.7 and 8.1 IU/L at the higher and lower dose in a trial of people taking warfarin (Parra 2007; Table 2's means give 18.3 for the higher dose), with no difference at that trial's last measurement.

The protocol was not registered and no assessment of bias in the trials was done. The review was funded by an investigator-initiated grant from McNeil Consumer Healthcare to Denver Health; the sponsors are stated to have had no role in design, performance, analysis or authorship, but the sponsor reviewed the final manuscript. Five authors are Denver Health employees, and Denver Health has contracts with McNeil and Cadence (acetaminophen makers) and Cumberland (IV acetylcysteine maker); one author consulted for McNeil on behalf of Denver Health and testified for McNeil in 2010 litigation; review authors are authors of all five pooled trials.
